extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students studying patent infringement doctrine
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for deciding whether one machine infringes another's patent — focusing on substantial identity of principle, combinations, equivalents, and when differences amount to a new invention. Synthesizes judicial instructions and examples for fact-finders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial identity of principle/mode of operation
rubrics_metrics.description: The material question is not whether the same elements or component parts are used, but whether the given effect is produced substantially by the same mode of operation and the same combination of powers in both machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mere colorable differences or slight improvements cannot defeat the original inventor's right. Example: successive additions to a watch (minutes/seconds) by different parties using the same combinations and mode of operation do not give later patentees rights over the original invention beyond their own distinct contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form versus substance: same principle in effect
rubrics_metrics.description: One machine is the same in substance as another if the principle be the same in effect, though the form of the machine be different.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apparent differences in appearance or orientation (e.g., acting upwards vs downwards) do not avoid infringement where the underlying principle is the same (Boville v. Moore illustration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that defendant show 'substantially and materially different' construction
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid infringement the defendants must satisfy the fact-finder that their contrivance is substantially and materially different from the plaintiff's, i.e., that it involves some new idea in its construction not found in the plaintiff's.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the new idea is found in the defendant's machine it is appropriation; if not, it is an independent improvement and not a violation. Whether differences are merely formal or important is a factual inquiry for the jury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination test — presence of means or combination from prior machine
rubrics_metrics.description: The question is whether the later machine contains the means or combination found in the previous machine; if the combination of the prior machine is substantially incorporated, the defendant's mechanical differences are treated as equivalents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if mechanical structure differs, if the new idea/combination is embodied in the later device it is an infringement (Blanchard v. Beers). Look to whether the new device appropriates the ideas that gave value to the prior machine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention versus mere mechanical skill
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed departure from an existing machine must involve invention (mind and inventive genius) and not merely the superior mechanical skill of a workman to reorganize or adapt the machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the defendant's changes are the product of a mechanic's study and reorganization to adapt performance (not an inventive advance), that will not avoid infringement; the defendant must show inventive genius to claim a separate patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performance superiority not dispositive
rubrics_metrics.description: A defendant's machine being able to perform more rapidly or efficiently does not, by itself, avoid infringement if the principle or combination is substantially the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superior results may stem from superior construction, adaptation to a single purpose, or an actual improvement — but superiority alone doesn't entitle the defendant to use the prior principle or combination without authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption of sub-combinations and general arrangement may infringe
rubrics_metrics.description: If a later machine adopts the general combination and arrangement and some of the sub-combinations of the patentee's machine, it may constitute infringement even without exact replication of all minutiae.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will examine whether key sub-combinations and the general plan are present; experts' testimony that sub-combinations are identical is relevant (Howe/ Williams/ Sloat examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Material alteration of structure avoids infringement (when substantial)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the differences are not mere form but constitute a material alteration of structure — substantially different combinations of mechanism effecting the same purpose by means not the same in substance — then the later device is not an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a factual question for the jury; examples include materially different valve shapes/arrangements that render the constructions substantially different in substance (Lowell v. Lewis).

rubrics_metrics.name: Different methods accomplishing same object can be noninfringing
rubrics_metrics.description: Two devices that accomplish a well-known object by materially different methods (even if both use the common principle of rotating vanes) may each be new and noninfringing of the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an axial screw-vane forcing air through the stone eye vs removing a circular portion and using a centrifugal fan — held to be different inventions (distinct methods of accomplishing air flow).

rubrics_metrics.name: Protection for combinations producing a new and useful result
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual inventors of a combination of two or more ingredients are entitled to treat every one as an infringer who makes, uses, or vends the machine to be used without authority when the combination produces a new and useful result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle grants patentees protection even where ingredients are old, but is balanced: patentees cannot suppress subsequent improvements that are substantially different; mere formal alterations do not avoid infringement if substituted ingredient performs substantially the same function and was a well-known substitute at the patent date (Seymour v. Osborne).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of doctrine of equivalents for combination patents
rubrics_metrics.description: While patentees may invoke equivalents, they cannot use the doctrine to suppress all other substantial improvements; and for combination patents the patentee cannot treat someone as infringer unless the latter's machine contains all material ingredients of the prior combination (except where a substituted ingredient was a well-known substitute performing the same function).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule must be limited to avoid stifling later substantial innovations; the inventor of a combination has protection against colorable evasions but not against bona fide, substantially different improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination patent not infringed when an element is dispensed with and a substantially different substitute used
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent for a combination of several elements is not infringed by a combination which dispenses with one of the elements and substitutes therefor another substantially different in construction and operation, even if serving the same purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substituting an element that is substantially different in construction/operation (not a mere equivalent) can avoid infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacture/sale of parts can be infringement when parts are useless alone and sold for combination
rubrics_metrics.description: It may be infringement to manufacture and sell some parts of a patented combination if those parts are useless without the remaining parts and are sold with the understanding and intention that the remaining parts will be supplied by another and the whole combined for use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concerted action or implied agreement to bring the patented combination into use (each supplying a necessary useless component) can make sellers joint infringers liable for damages (Wallace v. Holmes). Non-joinder of all actors is not a defense where concert is inferable from the nature of the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fewer elements than claimed (when patent claims only the combination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a patent claims only a combination of known elements, the use of some but not all of those elements (i.e., fewer than all) is generally not an infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rule is subject to the exception that substituting equivalents or omitting immaterial parts will not always avoid infringement; the central question remains whether the machines are substantially the same.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of the patented principle (non-combination patents)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patent is for a principle (not merely a combination), and the defendant applies the principle in the same way as the patentee, absence of certain items mentioned in the specification will not prevent recovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the imitation is so nearly exact as to show an attempt to copy with only imperceptible variations to evade the patent, courts may disregard those slight variations as fraud and treat it as infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: When form and substance are inseparable: patent covers particular form only
rubrics_metrics.description: When the form described is the only form capable of embodying the invention, the patent may cover only that particular geometrical or structural form; if the form is not copied, the invention is not used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether form and substance are inseparable; if so, analyzing form alone may be sufficient to determine infringement (example: circular vs octagonal car where evidence showed practical equivalence versus cases where only one form can embody the invention).
